newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia PM appeals to parliament to end agony.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia PM appeals to parliament to end agony.

text.p: Slovenia's parliament looked set to back centre-left Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek as head of a new government on Thursday after a defection by a rightwinger almost ensured him an absolute majority.
"I appeal to you that we try to find a way out of this deadlock together," Drnovsek told parliament.
"If no other solution is found, then early elections are a better possibility than a continuation of this agony and political instability," he added.
A parliamentary vote on Drnovsek's mandate was expected to begin later on Thursday.
Rightwing leaders denounced a Christian Democrat defector in the parliamentary debate and said they would not support a new Drnovsek administration.

"Counting on one vote of a man who can betray basic moral principles does not lead to a reliable government," declared Christian Democrat Lojze Peterle, who was Slovenia's first prime minister after independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
Drnovsek, prime minister for the past four years, replied to criticism made by the so-called "Spring" alliance of three rightwing parties of his record on economic and social policy.

He acknowledged that his government had not been able to achieve all it had set out to do, but Slovenia had maintained its position as one of the best performing economies of Europe's former communist states.
November's general election left Slovenia with a hung parliament in which Drnovsek's Liberal Democrats and their allies had 45 out of 90 votes.

The rightwing alliance, comprising the conservative People's Party, centre-right Social Democrats and Christian Democrats, together won 45 seats in the election, but Wednesday's defection by Christian Democrat Ciril Pucko reduced its total by one.
According to the newspaper Dnevnik, police have had to provide special security for Pucko's family because of threats made to them since his defection.

Rightwing parties accused the Liberal Democrats of corruption, claiming they had offered large financial inducements to members of the Social Democrats to try to win their support of Drnovsek. The Liberal Democrats denied the accusations.
